questions.explanation: In each case a particle crosses a region where its energy is below the potential: the vacuum gap's work-function barrier, the Coulomb barrier around a nucleus (escaping in alpha decay, entering in fusion), or an insulating oxide in a memory cell.

questions.stem: An electron tunnels through a rectangular barrier. Which changes, made one at a time, increase the tunneling probability? Select all that apply.
choices: Using a heavier particle with the same energy
Raising the electron's energy, still below the top
questions.explanation: $T \approx e^{-2\kappa L}$ with $\kappa = \sqrt{2m(U - E)}/\hbar$. A thinner barrier reduces $L$; a lower barrier or a higher energy reduces $U - E$. A heavier particle increases $\kappa$ and lowers $T$.

questions.stem: The picture shows a wave function meeting a rectangular barrier (schematic). Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A rectangular barrier stands on a horizontal axis, with a dashed horizontal line below its top. A large wave on the left reaches the barrier, a smoothly falling curve crosses the barrier, and a small wave continues on the right. A double arrow spans the barrier's width.

choices: Turning point of the transmitted wave
Region where the particle loses energy
questions.explanation: On the left (1) the incoming and reflected waves combine. Inside the barrier (2), where $U > E$, the wave function decays exponentially (3) over the width $L$ (5). On the right (4) it continues as a smaller wave with the same wavelength: same energy, lower probability. Nowhere does the particle lose energy.

questions.stem: Uranium-238 (238.050788 u) alpha decays to thorium-234 (234.043601 u). Helium-4 is 4.002603 u. What is the Q-value? (1 u = 931.5 MeV/$c^2$)
questions.explanation: $\Delta m = 238.050788 - 234.043601 - 4.002603 = 0.004584$ u, and $Q = 0.004584(931.5) = 4.27$ MeV. 4.20 MeV is the alpha particle's share, $4.27(234/238)$; 0.00458 is the mass difference in u, not MeV; 3730 MeV is the rest energy of the whole helium-4 atom, not the energy released.

questions.stem: Polonium-210 alpha decays at rest with $Q = 5.41$ MeV. What is the alpha particle's kinetic energy?
questions.explanation: Equal and opposite momenta give $K_\alpha = Q(A - 4)/A = 5.41(206/210) = 5.31$ MeV. The lead-206 nucleus recoils with the remaining 0.10 MeV. Giving all of $Q$ to the alpha particle ignores the recoil; 0.10 MeV is the recoil's share, given to the wrong particle; 2.71 MeV splits $Q$ evenly, which equal momenta do not do for unequal masses.

questions.stem: Using atomic masses, when is beta-plus decay energetically possible?
choices: Whenever the parent atom is heavier than the daughter atom
Only when the daughter atom is heavier
Whenever the parent nucleus has more protons than neutrons
When the parent atom outweighs the daughter atom by more than $2m_e = 1.022$ MeV/$c^2$
questions.explanation: With atomic masses, $Q_{\beta^+} = (M_{\text{parent}} - M_{\text{daughter}})c^2 - 2m_ec^2$: one electron mass because the daughter atom has one fewer electron, and one for the positron created. Electron capture needs only $M_{\text{parent}} > M_{\text{daughter}}$, so it can occur where β⁺ cannot.

questions.stem: Deuterium–tritium fusion releases 17.6 MeV, shared between a helium-4 nucleus and a neutron (initial kinetic energy negligible). How much does the neutron carry?
questions.explanation: Equal momenta mean energies in inverse ratio to mass: the neutron (mass number 1) gets $\tfrac45$ of 17.6 MeV $= 14.1$ MeV, and the helium nucleus gets 3.5 MeV. Splitting evenly gives 8.8 MeV, 3.5 MeV is the helium nucleus's share, and 17.6 MeV ignores the helium nucleus's recoil.

questions.stem: In the liquid-drop model, which term is mainly responsible for the fall in binding energy per nucleon among heavy nuclei?
questions.explanation: The Coulomb term grows as $Z^2/A^{1/3}$, roughly as $A^{5/3}$, faster than the volume term's $A$, so per nucleon it keeps growing. The surface term matters most for light nuclei; the pairing term is only about 1 MeV.

questions.stem: The line of stability is $Z \approx A/(2 + 0.0150A^{2/3})$. What does it predict for $A = 120$?
questions.explanation: $120^{2/3} = 24.3$, so $Z \approx 120/(2 + 0.364) = 50.7$, about 51. Tin ($Z = 50$) has several stable isotopes near $A = 120$. $Z = 60$ is the naive $A/2$, which ignores the Coulomb term. Using $A$ instead of $A^{2/3}$ gives $120/3.80 = 32$; using $A^{1/3}$ gives $120/2.074 = 58$.

questions.stem: In the semi-empirical mass formula, which nucleus gets the pairing bonus $+\delta$?
questions.explanation: Calcium-40 has $Z = 20$ and $N = 20$, both even: $+\delta$. Potassium-40 has $Z = 19$, $N = 21$, both odd: $-\delta$. Potassium-39 and aluminum-27 have odd $A$: pairing term 0.

questions.stem: A nuclear reaction has $Q = -2.0$ MeV. What does this mean?
choices: It releases 2.0 MeV of kinetic energy
It can occur only if the colliding particles bring in at least 2.0 MeV of kinetic energy, and in fact somewhat more
The products have 2.0 MeV less rest energy than the reactants
questions.explanation: Negative $Q$ means the products have more rest energy than the reactants, so kinetic energy must be supplied. Because momentum is also conserved, some kinetic energy stays in the motion of the products, so the beam needs more than $|Q|$.

questions.stem: In the semi-empirical mass formula the surface term is proportional to $A$ raised to the power ___.
questions.explanation: The radius goes as $A^{1/3}$, so the surface area goes as $R^2 \propto A^{2/3}$.

questions.stem: Fission of one uranium-235 nucleus releases about ___ MeV. Give only the number, to 1 significant figure.
questions.explanation: Binding energy per nucleon rises from about 7.6 MeV to about 8.5 MeV when uranium splits into medium-mass fragments: roughly $(0.9)(236) \approx 200$ MeV, in agreement with measurement.

questions.stem: For iron-56, put the terms of the semi-empirical mass formula in order from largest to smallest magnitude.
questions.explanation: With the lesson's coefficients: volume $+882.0$ MeV, surface $-260.5$, Coulomb $-120.8$, asymmetry $-6.8$ (iron-56 has only 4 more neutrons than protons), pairing $+1.5$.

questions.stem: Match each term of the semi-empirical mass formula to its physical origin.
choices: Each nucleon is bound to its nearest neighbors
Nucleons at the edge have fewer neighbors
The exclusion principle penalizes unequal numbers of protons and neutrons
Paired nucleons are more tightly bound
questions.explanation: These are the five ingredients of the liquid-drop picture. Gravity between nucleons is negligibly weak compared with the nuclear and electric forces and plays no part.

questions.stem: For which processes can the Q-value be found from atomic masses directly, with no extra electron-mass correction? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: In alpha decay, beta-minus decay and electron capture the electron counts work out when atomic masses are used on both sides. In beta-plus decay the daughter atom has one fewer electron and a positron is created, so subtract $2m_ec^2 = 1.022$ MeV.

questions.stem: Put the steps for charging a neutral metal sphere positively by induction, using a negatively charged rod, in order.
choices: Hold the negative rod near the sphere without touching it
Connect the sphere to ground with a wire
questions.explanation: The rod polarizes the sphere, and grounding lets electrons pushed away by the rod escape to Earth. The ground must be removed while the rod is still there: if the rod went first, electrons would flow back up the wire and the sphere would end up neutral. Once the ground is gone, removing the rod leaves the sphere with a net positive charge, which spreads over its surface.

questions.stem: Two point charges exert a force of 0.80 N on each other. If the distance between them is halved, the force becomes ___ N. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $F \propto 1/r^2$, so halving $r$ multiplies the force by $2^2 = 4$: $4(0.80) = 3.2$ N. (Doubling to 1.6 N forgets to square.)

questions.stem: Which statements about electric charge are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The total charge of an isolated system never changes
Rubbing two objects together creates new charge
A charged object can attract a neutral one
Every free charge is a whole-number multiple of $e$
Two negative charges attract each other
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved and quantized ($q = ne$), and a charged object attracts a neutral one by polarizing it. Rubbing only moves electrons from one object to the other; it creates no net charge. Like charges, including two negatives, repel.

questions.stem: Classify each material as it behaves at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Metals such as copper, and salt water (with its free ions), let charge move: conductors. Rubber and dry air hold charges in place: insulators. Silicon is the standard semiconductor, in between.

questions.stem: Charges of $+2.0$ μC sit at $x = 0$ and at $x = 0.40$ m. Find the net force on a $+1.0$ μC charge at $x = 0.10$ m, as a signed $x$ component in newtons to 2 significant figures ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²). $F_x =$ ___ N. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: The charge at 0 is 0.10 m away and repels toward $+x$: $(8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})(1.0\times10^{-6})/(0.10)^2 = 1.80$ N. The charge at 0.40 m is 0.30 m away and repels toward $-x$: $1.80/9 = 0.20$ N. Net $F_x = 1.80 - 0.20 = 1.6$ N. Adding the magnitudes gives 2.0 N, the mistake of ignoring directions.

questions.stem: This is the setup for steering an electron beam, as in an old cathode-ray tube. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A box at the left fires a dashed path to the right between two horizontal plates, the top plate marked with plus signs and the bottom one with minus signs. Arrows between the plates point down. The path curves upward between the plates, then runs straight to a tall vertical bar at the right.

questions.explanation: 1 is the electron gun that produces the beam. 2 is the top plate, marked +, the positive deflection plate. 3 is the uniform field between the plates, pointing from the positive plate to the negative one. 4 is the straight path after the electron leaves the plates (no field acts there), and 5 is the screen where the beam lands. The negative plate is the bottom one, which has no marker.

questions.stem: The electric field 0.30 m from a $+6.0$ nC point charge is about ___ N/C (2 significant figures, $k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²). Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $E = kq/r^2 = (8.99\times10^9)(6.0\times10^{-9})/(0.30)^2 = 599$ N/C, or 600 N/C to 2 significant figures, pointing away from the charge. Forgetting to square $r$ gives 180 N/C.

questions.stem: A metal object is in electrostatic equilibrium. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The electric field inside the metal is zero
Any excess charge sits on the outer surface
Just outside, the field is parallel to the surface
Charge concentrates where the surface curves most sharply
Excess charge spreads evenly through the volume of the metal
questions.explanation: If there were a field inside the metal, free charges would still be moving, so $E = 0$ inside, and excess charge ends up on the outer surface, crowding at sharp points. Just outside, the field is perpendicular to the surface; a parallel component would push charge along the surface.

questions.stem: Match each charge distribution to how its electric field behaves.
left: Center of a uniformly charged ring
questions.explanation: Point charge $kq/r^2$; line $2k\lambda/r$; sheet $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$, independent of distance. At a ring's center every element's field is canceled by the element opposite it. The $1/r^3$ falloff belongs to a dipole, which isn't listed.

questions.stem: An electron moves horizontally into the space between two horizontal plates; the top plate is positive and the bottom plate negative. While it is between the plates, its path
choices: is a straight line, since the field is uniform
bends up in a circular arc
bends up in a parabola, toward the positive plate
questions.explanation: The field points down (from $+$ to $-$), and an electron is pushed opposite to the field, so it feels a constant upward force. Constant force across a sideways velocity gives a parabola, as for a thrown ball. Bending down would be correct for a positive charge; a circular arc needs a force that keeps turning, as in a magnetic field.

questions.stem: Each dashed surface is the Gaussian surface used for the charge it surrounds. Name each one.

image.alt: Three panels. Left: a solid ball inside a dashed circle with arrows pointing outward all around. Middle: a vertical line of plus charges inside a dashed cylinder, with arrows pointing sideways out of its curved side. Right: a slanted flat sheet of plus charges pierced by a short dashed cylinder, with arrows pointing out of its two ends.

questions.explanation: A spherical charge uses a concentric sphere ($E\cdot4\pi r^2$), a long line uses a coaxial cylinder (flux only through the curved side, $E\cdot2\pi rL$), and a flat sheet uses a pillbox through the sheet (flux only through the two end caps, $E\cdot2A$). In each case $E$ is constant on the parts of the surface the field crosses.

questions.stem: A closed surface surrounds a $+5.0$ nC charge and a $-2.0$ nC charge; a $+4.0$ nC charge sits outside it. The net electric flux through the surface is ___ N·m²/C, to 3 significant figures ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²)). Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Only enclosed charge counts: $Q_{\text{enc}} = 5.0 - 2.0 = 3.0$ nC, so $\Phi_E = (3.0\times10^{-9})/(8.85\times10^{-12}) = 339$ N·m²/C. Including the outside charge would give 791.

questions.stem: Put the steps for finding a field with Gauss's law in order.
choices: Identify the symmetry of the charge distribution
Choose a Gaussian surface through the point, on which E is constant
Set E times the area it crosses equal to the enclosed charge over ε0
questions.explanation: The symmetry decides the surface (sphere, cylinder or pillbox); the surface must pass through the point where you want $E$ and have $E$ constant and perpendicular wherever field crosses it. Then the flux is $E$ times that area, Gauss's law sets it equal to $Q_{\text{enc}}/\varepsilon_0$, and you solve for $E$.

questions.stem: For which charge distributions does Gauss's law, with a well-chosen surface, give the field directly? Select all that apply.
choices: A very long, uniformly charged straight wire
A very large, flat, uniformly charged sheet
questions.explanation: Spherical, cylindrical and planar symmetry let you pick a surface with $E$ constant on it. A cube's field and a dipole's field vary in magnitude and direction over any simple closed surface. Gauss's law is still true for them, but it doesn't hand you $E$.

questions.stem: Inside a uniformly charged solid ball, the field at half the radius is ___ times the field at the surface. Give the number as a fraction or decimal.
questions.explanation: Inside, $E = kQr/R^3$ grows in proportion to $r$, so at $r = R/2$ the field is half the surface value $kQ/R^2$. (Using $kQ/r^2$ inside would wrongly give 4 times.)

questions.stem: The picture shows two charged parallel plates. Name the numbered features.

image.alt: Two vertical plates, the left one marked with plus signs and the right one with minus signs. Horizontal arrows run from the left plate to the right plate, and three evenly spaced dashed vertical lines lie between the plates.

questions.explanation: The field points from high potential to low, so the positive left plate is at the higher potential and the right plate at the lower one. The arrows are field lines; the dashed lines, perpendicular to them, are equipotentials. Moving along an equipotential takes no work.

questions.stem: A proton starts from rest and is accelerated through a potential difference of 2000 V. It gains ___ eV of kinetic energy. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: A charge $e$ moving through $\Delta V$ gains $e|\Delta V|$ of kinetic energy: 2000 eV $= 3.2\times10^{-16}$ J. That is the point of the electron volt; the proton's mass doesn't enter (it affects the speed, not the energy).

questions.stem: Match each quantity to its SI unit.
questions.explanation: Potential is energy per charge, J/C = V. Potential energy is an energy, in joules. The field is force per charge, N/C, which equals V/m. The farad (C/V) is the unit of capacitance.

questions.stem: Which statements about equipotential surfaces are true? Select all that apply.
choices: They are perpendicular to the field lines
The field points from low potential toward high potential
Moving a charge along one takes no work
Around a point charge they are parallel planes
The field is strongest where they are closest together
questions.explanation: No work is done along an equipotential, so the field has no component along it: field lines cross equipotentials at right angles, and closely spaced equipotentials mean a steep potential, a strong field. The field points from high to low potential, and a point charge's equipotentials are concentric spheres.

questions.stem: In a region the potential is $V(x) = 5x^2$ volts, with $x$ in meters. What is the field at $x = 2$ m?
questions.explanation: $E_x = -dV/dx = -10x = -20$ V/m at $x = 2$: the field points toward $-x$, down the potential slope. $+20$ V/m forgets the minus sign; $-10$ V/m is $-dV/dx$ evaluated at $x = 1$ instead of 2.

questions.stem: A water molecule is a permanent dipole. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A large circle bonded to two smaller circles that hang below it on either side, forming a bent shape. To the right, a vertical arrow points downward.

questions.explanation: The large atom is oxygen, which pulls the shared electrons toward itself and becomes slightly negative; the two hydrogens are slightly positive. The dipole moment points from the negative end to the positive end, from the oxygen toward the hydrogens. Water's dipole is permanent, not induced.

questions.stem: A dipole consists of charges $\pm3.0$ nC held 4.0 mm apart. Its dipole moment is ___ $\times10^{-12}$ C·m. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $p = qd = (3.0\times10^{-9})(4.0\times10^{-3}) = 1.2\times10^{-11} = 12\times10^{-12}$ C·m. Using the total charge, 6.0 nC, would double it.

questions.stem: A dipole sits in a uniform field at angle θ between $\vec p$ and $\vec E$. Match each angle to what is true there.
questions.explanation: $U = -pE\cos\theta$ is lowest ($-pE$) when aligned and highest ($+pE$) when antiparallel; both have zero torque, but only the aligned one is stable. The torque $pE\sin\theta$ peaks at $90^\circ$. In a uniform field the net force is zero at every angle.

questions.stem: A small dipole is placed in a uniform electric field at an angle to it. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The net force on it is zero
It accelerates toward the stronger field
The torque turns $\vec p$ toward $\vec E$
Its own field far away falls off as $1/r^2$
questions.explanation: The forces on $+q$ and $-q$ are equal and opposite (zero net force) but form a couple, $\vec\tau = \vec p\times\vec E$, which swings $\vec p$ toward $\vec E$; $U = -\vec p\cdot\vec E$. A uniform field has no stronger region to move toward, and a dipole's own far field falls off as $1/r^3$.

questions.stem: Rank the strength of a small dipole's field at these points, strongest first. All distances are measured from the dipole's center and are much larger than its length.
choices: 2 cm away on the perpendicular bisector
4 cm away on the perpendicular bisector
questions.explanation: On the axis $E \approx 2kp/r^3$, on the bisector $kp/r^3$. In units of $kp/(1\text{ cm})^3$: axis at 2 cm $2/8 = 0.25$; bisector at 2 cm $1/8 = 0.125$; axis at 4 cm $2/64 \approx 0.031$; bisector at 4 cm $1/64 \approx 0.016$. Doubling the distance cuts the field by 8, more than the factor of 2 between axis and bisector.

questions.stem: A dielectric fills the gap of a charged capacitor (top plate positive). Name the numbered features.

image.alt: Two horizontal plates with a shaded slab between them. Plus signs sit above the top plate and minus signs below the bottom plate. Inside the slab, a row of minus signs lines the top surface and a row of plus signs lines the bottom surface; between them are oval molecules, each with a minus sign at its top and a plus sign at its bottom. A large arrow at the left points down.

questions.explanation: 1 is the free charge delivered to the plate by the battery. 4 is the field, pointing from the positive plate to the negative one. The molecules (3) are polarized along it, negative ends up. Their charges cancel inside the slab but not at its surfaces, leaving bound charge (2) that faces the plate of opposite sign and partly cancels its field. No charge flows through an insulator.

questions.stem: A 4.0 μF capacitor and a 12 μF capacitor are connected in series. Their equivalent capacitance is ___ μF. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $1/C_{\text{eq}} = 1/4.0 + 1/12 = 4/12$, so $C_{\text{eq}} = 3.0$ μF, smaller than either. Adding them (16 μF) is the parallel rule.

questions.stem: Rank these from smallest to largest capacitance.
choices: A 2.0 μF and a 4.0 μF capacitor in series
A 2.0 μF and a 4.0 μF capacitor in parallel
questions.explanation: Series: $1/(1/2 + 1/4) = 1.33$ μF, below the smaller one. Parallel: $2 + 4 = 6$ μF, above the larger one. So 1.33 < 2.0 < 4.0 < 6.0 μF.

questions.stem: Which changes increase the capacitance of a parallel-plate capacitor? Select all that apply.
choices: Putting more charge on the plates
Filling the gap with a dielectric
questions.explanation: $C = \kappa\varepsilon_0A/d$ depends only on the geometry and the material between the plates: larger $A$, smaller $d$ and larger $\kappa$ all raise it. Raising $V$ raises $Q$ in proportion, so $C = Q/V$ is unchanged.

questions.stem: Match each formula to what it gives.
choices: Energy per volume of an electric field
questions.explanation: Parallel plates: $\varepsilon_0A/d$. Stored energy: $\tfrac12CV^2$ ($= \tfrac12QV = Q^2/2C$). The field's energy density is $\tfrac12\varepsilon_0E^2$. Reciprocals add for series; for parallel the capacitances themselves add, $C_1 + C_2$.

questions.stem: Where does the electric potential satisfy Laplace's equation, $\nabla^2V = 0$?
choices: At every point in any region, charged or not
At every point where there is no charge
Only where the field is uniform
questions.explanation: Poisson's equation $\nabla^2V = -\rho/\varepsilon_0$ holds everywhere; it reduces to Laplace's equation wherever $\rho = 0$. That includes the empty space around charges and the inside of conductors (where $V$ is constant), so "only inside conductors" is too narrow, and a nonuniform field in empty space still satisfies it.

questions.stem: According to Earnshaw's theorem, which of these can hold a charged particle in stable equilibrium?
choices: A static electric field combined with a magnetic field
A cleverly arranged set of fixed point charges
A charged ring, with the particle at its center
The field inside a charged hollow metal sphere
questions.explanation: A static electric field alone has no potential minimum in empty space (Laplace's equation forbids one), so fixed charges can give at best a saddle point. The ring's center is stable along the axis or across it, never both. Inside a charged hollow sphere the field is zero, so the particle is in neutral, not stable, equilibrium. Adding a magnetic field, as in a Penning trap, gets around the theorem.

questions.stem: A closed, empty metal box sits in a strong external field. Which argument shows that the field inside is exactly zero?
choices: The outside charges are too far away to matter
The box's walls absorb the field lines
The induced charges inside the cavity cancel the field only approximately
A constant potential fits Laplace's equation and the walls, so by uniqueness it is the solution
questions.explanation: The walls are one conductor, so they are at one potential $V_0$. $V = V_0$ throughout the cavity satisfies $\nabla^2V = 0$ and matches the boundary, and the uniqueness theorem says it is the only solution, so $E = -\nabla V = 0$ exactly. The external field can be as close or as strong as you like.

questions.stem: A $+3.0$ nC charge is 2.0 cm above a large grounded metal plate. What force does the plate exert on it? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: The image is $-3.0$ nC at 2.0 cm below the surface, 4.0 cm from the charge: $F = kq^2/(2d)^2 = (8.99\times10^9)(3.0\times10^{-9})^2/(0.040)^2 = 5.1\times10^{-5}$ N, an attraction. Using $d$ instead of $2d$ gives $2.0\times10^{-4}$ N; forgetting to square $2d$ gives $2.0\times10^{-6}$ N.

questions.stem: A $+5.0$ nC charge is 4.0 cm above a large grounded conducting plane. Its image is a ___ nC charge located ___ cm below the plane. Give only the numbers, with a sign on the charge.
questions.explanation: The image of $+q$ at height $d$ is $-q$ at the mirror point, depth $d$: $-5.0$ nC, 4.0 cm below the surface. Then every point of the plane is equally far from the two charges and $V = 0$ there.

questions.stem: A $+2.0$ nC charge is 1.0 cm above a grounded plane. What is the induced surface charge density on the plane directly beneath it?
questions.explanation: At $r = 0$, $\sigma = -\dfrac{qd}{2\pi(d^2)^{3/2}} = -\dfrac{q}{2\pi d^2} = -\dfrac{2.0\times10^{-9}}{2\pi(0.010)^2} = -3.2\times10^{-6}$ C/m². The induced charge is opposite in sign to $q$. Using $4\pi$ or $\pi$ in place of $2\pi$ gives the other magnitudes.

questions.stem: How much work does it take to pull a $+4.0$ nC charge from 2.0 cm above a large grounded plate to very far away? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: The force at height $x$ is $kq^2/(4x^2)$, and $\int_d^\infty kq^2/(4x^2)\,dx = kq^2/(4d) = (8.99\times10^9)(4.0\times10^{-9})^2/(0.080) = 1.8\times10^{-6}$ J. $3.6\times10^{-6}$ J is $kq^2/(2d)$, the energy of a real pair $2d$ apart, which overcounts because the image moves along with the charge and the field fills only half of space. $7.2\times10^{-6}$ J is $kq^2/d$, and $9.0\times10^{-7}$ J is $kq^2/(8d)$, half the right value.

questions.stem: A $+8.0$ nC charge is 40 cm from the center of a grounded metal sphere of radius 10 cm. The image charge is ___ nC, located ___ cm from the sphere's center. Give only the numbers, with a sign on the charge.
questions.explanation: $q' = -qR/a = -(8.0)(10/40) = -2.0$ nC, at $b = R^2/a = 100/40 = 2.5$ cm from the center, on the line toward the charge.

questions.stem: A $+8.0$ nC charge is 40 cm from the center of a grounded metal sphere of radius 10 cm, so its image is $-2.0$ nC at 2.5 cm from the center. What is the magnitude of the force on the charge? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: The charges are $40 - 2.5 = 37.5$ cm apart: $F = (8.99\times10^9)(8.0\times10^{-9})(2.0\times10^{-9})/(0.375)^2 = 1.0\times10^{-6}$ N, attractive. Using the distance to the center (40 cm) gives $8.99\times10^{-7}$ N, the distance to the surface (30 cm) $1.6\times10^{-6}$ N, and an image of $-8.0$ nC $4.1\times10^{-6}$ N.

questions.stem: Which statements about the method of images are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Image charges are placed outside the region where the field is wanted
The total induced charge on a grounded plane equals $-q$
Inside the metal, the true field equals the image charge's field
A grounded sphere's image charge is smaller in magnitude than the real charge
The image charge is a real charge that collects at one point in the metal
questions.explanation: The images sit outside the region, so the region's charges are just the real ones and uniqueness applies. Integrating $\sigma$ over the plane gives exactly $-q$; a sphere's image $-qR/a$ is smaller because $R < a$. Inside the metal the true field is zero, and the real induced charge is spread over the surface; the image is only a calculating device.

questions.stem: Put the steps of the method of images in order.
choices: Choose the region where you want the field
Place image charges outside that region
Check that the conductor's surface has the required potential
Compute the force and the induced surface charge
questions.explanation: The region must be fixed before you know where images may go (outside it). Only after checking the boundary condition can you appeal to uniqueness, and only then are the field, forces and $\sigma = \varepsilon_0E_\perp$ trustworthy.

questions.stem: Match each conductor problem to the image charges that solve it (q is the real charge).
left: Charge at height d above a grounded plane
Charge at distance a from the center of a grounded sphere of radius R
The same sphere but isolated and neutral
choices: −q at depth d below the plane
−qR/a at distance R²/a from the center
The grounded-sphere image plus +qR/a at the center
−q at the center of the sphere
questions.explanation: A mirror image for the plane; for a grounded sphere, $-qR/a$ at $R^2/a$ makes every point of the sphere's surface have $V = 0$. A neutral isolated sphere must carry zero net charge, so $+qR/a$ is added at the center, which keeps the surface an equipotential. A charge $-q$ at the center does not make the surface an equipotential.

questions.stem: The picture shows a charge above a flat metal surface, with the image used to find its field. Name the numbered features.

image.alt: A small circle with a plus sign sits above a horizontal hatched surface. Curved lines with arrows leave it; some go up and out, and the rest curve down to meet the surface at right angles. A dashed circle with a minus sign is drawn the same distance below the surface, joined to the upper circle by a dashed vertical line.

questions.explanation: 1 is the real charge $+q$ and 2 the image $-q$, drawn dashed because nothing is really there. 3 is the grounded metal surface, which the field lines (4) meet at right angles, as they must at a conductor's surface, an equipotential.

questions.stem: Using the image model, what is the potential energy of an electron 1.0 nm from a flat metal surface? ($ke^2 = 1.44$ eV·nm)
questions.explanation: $U = -ke^2/(4x) = -1.44/(4 \times 1.0) = -0.36$ eV. $-0.72$ eV is $-ke^2/(2x)$, the pair-energy mistake; $-1.44$ eV forgets the factor of 4 entirely; $-0.18$ eV uses $8x$.

questions.stem: The polarization $\vec P$ of a dielectric is measured in
questions.explanation: $\vec P$ is dipole moment per volume: (C·m)/m³ = C/m², the unit of surface charge density, which fits $\sigma_b = \vec P\cdot\hat n$. C·m is a single dipole moment; C/m³ is a volume charge density.

questions.stem: A dielectric slab fills a capacitor. The bound charge on the face of the slab touching the positive plate is
choices: positive, equal to the free charge
negative, smaller in magnitude than the free charge
zero, because the slab is neutral
negative, larger in magnitude than the free charge
questions.explanation: The dipoles point along $\vec E$, away from the positive plate, so their negative ends face it: $\sigma_b = -\sigma_f(1 - 1/\kappa)$, opposite in sign and smaller in size. The slab is neutral overall because the far face carries the opposite bound charge. If it exceeded the free charge, the field would reverse inside.

questions.stem: A dielectric with $\kappa = 4.0$ fills a capacitor whose plates carry free charge density $2.0$ μC/m². What is the magnitude of the bound surface charge density on the dielectric?
questions.explanation: $\sigma_b = \sigma_f(1 - 1/\kappa) = 2.0(1 - 0.25) = 1.5$ μC/m². The net charge $\sigma_f - \sigma_b = 0.50$ μC/m² $= \sigma_f/\kappa$ is what sets the reduced field, a common mix-up.

questions.stem: A material has dielectric constant $\kappa = 2.5$. Its electric susceptibility $\chi_e$ is ___. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: $\kappa = 1 + \chi_e$, so $\chi_e = 1.5$. (Vacuum has $\chi_e = 0$, $\kappa = 1$.)

questions.stem: A dielectric slab lies flat against one plate of a charged capacitor, with air in the rest of the gap. Which quantity has the same value in the air and in the slab?
questions.explanation: A pillbox around the plate encloses only the plate's free charge, so $D = \sigma_f$ in both layers. $E = D/(\kappa\varepsilon_0)$ is $\kappa$ times smaller in the slab, $P$ is zero in the air, and the energy density $\tfrac12ED$ differs too.

questions.stem: Plates of area 0.010 m² are 3.0 mm apart. A slab with $\kappa = 2.0$ and thickness 1.0 mm lies against one plate. What is the capacitance? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²))
questions.explanation: $C = \varepsilon_0A/(d - t + t/\kappa) = (8.85\times10^{-14})/(0.0020 + 0.00050) = 35$ pF. Without the slab it is 30 pF; treating the gap as fully filled gives 59 pF; multiplying by $\kappa$ instead of dividing ($d - t + \kappa t$) gives 22 pF.

questions.stem: A charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and then a dielectric slab is slid in to fill it. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The charge on the plates increases
The voltage between the plates decreases
The slab is pushed out of the gap
questions.explanation: With $Q$ fixed, $C \to \kappa C$, $V = Q/C$ falls by $\kappa$, and $U = Q^2/(2C)$ falls by $\kappa$. The energy lost is the work the field does pulling the slab in, not pushing it out. With no battery, the charge cannot change.

questions.stem: A 10 pF capacitor stays connected to a 100 V battery while a slab with $\kappa = 4.0$ is slid in to fill it. How much energy does the battery supply?
questions.explanation: $Q$ rises from 1.0 nC to 4.0 nC, so the battery moves 3.0 nC through 100 V: 300 nJ. The stored energy rises from 50 nJ to 200 nJ, an increase of 150 nJ, half of what the battery supplied; the other 150 nJ is work done on the slab as it is pulled in.

questions.stem: Match each situation to the right description.
left: Slab slid into a capacitor disconnected from its battery
Slab slid into a capacitor kept on its battery
Slab against one plate with air in the rest of the gap
Slab of full thickness covering half the plate area
choices: Acts like two capacitors in series
Acts like two capacitors in parallel
Slab is pushed out of the gap
questions.explanation: Fixed $Q$: $U = Q^2/(2C)$ falls as $C$ grows. Fixed $V$: $U = \tfrac12CV^2$ rises. Stacked layers carry the same $D$ (same charge) and their voltages add, which is series; side-by-side regions share the voltage, which is parallel. In both insertion cases the slab is pulled in.

questions.stem: Dry air breaks down at about $3.0\times10^6$ V/m. The largest voltage that can be put across an air gap of 2.0 mm is about ___ V. Give only the number.
Two ions in a liquid with dielectric constant 25 are a fixed distance apart. Treating the liquid as a uniform dielectric, the force between them compared with the same ions in vacuum is
choices: unchanged, since force depends only on the charges and distance
questions.explanation: In a uniform linear dielectric $\varepsilon_0$ becomes $\kappa\varepsilon_0$, so $F = q_1q_2/(4\pi\kappa\varepsilon_0r^2)$, $\kappa$ times weaker. The bound charges around each ion partly screen it. (At molecular distances this smooth-dielectric model is only a rough guide.)

questions.stem: The same pair of plates, 4.0 mm apart, is used four ways. Rank the capacitances from smallest to largest.
choices: A slab 2.0 mm thick with κ = 3.0, air in the rest
A slab 2.0 mm thick with κ = 6.0, air in the rest
The whole gap filled with κ = 3.0
questions.explanation: $C \propto 1/(d - t + t/\kappa)$ in mm: air $1/4 = 0.25$; $1/(2 + 0.67) = 0.375$; $1/(2 + 0.33) = 0.43$; full gap $3/4 = 0.75$. A partial slab helps less than you might expect because the air layer still carries most of the voltage.

questions.stem: A dielectric has $\kappa = 2.0$ and dielectric strength $1.5\times10^7$ V/m. What is the most energy per cubic meter a capacitor using it can store?
questions.explanation: $u_{\max} = \tfrac12\kappa\varepsilon_0E_{\max}^2 = \tfrac12(2.0)(8.85\times10^{-12})(1.5\times10^7)^2 = 2.0\times10^3$ J/m³. Leaving out $\kappa$ gives $1.0\times10^3$; leaving out the $\tfrac12$ gives $4.0\times10^3$; forgetting to square $E$ gives $1.3\times10^{-4}$.

questions.stem: Plates 5.0 cm wide and 0.50 mm apart are held at 500 V. A slab with $\kappa = 3.0$ is partly inserted. With what force is it pulled in?
questions.explanation: $F = (\kappa - 1)\varepsilon_0wV^2/(2d) = (2.0)(8.85\times10^{-12})(0.050)(500)^2/(2 \times 0.00050) = 2.2\times10^{-4}$ N. Using $\kappa$ instead of $\kappa - 1$ gives $3.3\times10^{-4}$ N; dropping the 2 in the denominator gives $4.4\times10^{-4}$ N, and dividing by 2 twice gives $1.1\times10^{-4}$ N.

questions.stem: Three $+2.0$ μC charges sit at the corners of an equilateral triangle with 0.30 m sides. How much work did it take to assemble them? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: Three pairs, each $kq^2/r = (8.99\times10^9)(2.0\times10^{-6})^2/0.30 = 0.120$ J: total 0.36 J. One pair alone is 0.12 J; counting each pair twice gives 0.72 J; using $r^2$ gives 1.2 J.

questions.stem: To find the energy of five point charges with $U = \sum kq_iq_j/r_{ij}$, you add ___ pair terms. Give only the number.
questions.explanation: Each pair is counted once: $\binom52 = 5 \times 4/2 = 10$. Counting 20 counts every pair twice, which is why the other form, $\tfrac12\sum q_iV_i$, has a $\tfrac12$.

questions.stem: A thin shell and a uniformly charged solid ball have the same charge $Q$ and radius $R$. The ball's self-energy divided by the shell's is
questions.explanation: Ball $\tfrac35kQ^2/R$, shell $\tfrac12kQ^2/R$: ratio $0.6/0.5 = 1.2$. The ball also has field energy inside it, which the shell (with $E = 0$ inside) lacks.

questions.stem: What is the self-energy of a thin conducting spherical shell of radius 10 cm carrying 5.0 nC? ($k = 8.99\times10^9$ N·m²/C²)
questions.explanation: $U = kQ^2/(2R) = (8.99\times10^9)(5.0\times10^{-9})^2/(0.20) = 1.1\times10^{-6}$ J. Dropping the $\tfrac12$ gives $2.2\times10^{-6}$ J, the solid-ball formula $\tfrac35kQ^2/R$ gives $1.3\times10^{-6}$ J, and using the diameter (0.20 m) as $R$ gives $5.6\times10^{-7}$ J.

questions.stem: The classical electron radius $r_e = ke^2/(m_ec^2)$ is about ___ fm (2 significant figures). Give only the number.
Why is the classical electron radius not the actual size of the electron?
choices: It was calculated with an old, inaccurate value of $e$
Experiments find no structure in the electron down to scales far below it
The electron is larger, because its charge spreads through the atom
It ignores the electron's magnetic field, which doubles its size
questions.explanation: $r_e$ is only the radius at which a classical charge's electric energy would equal $m_ec^2$ (with a factor of order 1 dropped). Scattering experiments find the electron pointlike to far smaller distances. The value of $e$ is known very precisely, and the electron's spread in an atom is a quantum probability cloud, not its size.

questions.stem: Model an iron-56 nucleus ($Z = 26$) as a uniformly charged ball of radius $(1.2\text{ fm})A^{1/3} = 4.6$ fm. Using $ke^2 = 1.44$ MeV·fm, its electric self-energy is about
questions.explanation: $U = \tfrac35k(Ze)^2/R = 0.6(1.44)(26)^2/4.59 = 127$ MeV. Without the $\tfrac35$ it is 212 MeV; the shell formula ($\tfrac12$) gives 106 MeV; using $Z$ instead of $Z^2$ gives 4.9 MeV.

questions.stem: A conductor's surface carries $\sigma = 4.0$ μC/m². What is the electrostatic pressure on the surface? ($\varepsilon_0 = 8.85\times10^{-12}$ C²/(N·m²))
questions.explanation: $P = \sigma^2/(2\varepsilon_0) = (4.0\times10^{-6})^2/(1.77\times10^{-11}) = 0.90$ Pa, always outward (for either sign of charge). $\sigma^2/\varepsilon_0 = 1.8$ Pa uses the full outside field instead of the average; $2.3\times10^5$ Pa forgets to square $\sigma$.

questions.stem: A parallel-plate capacitor holds charge $Q$, and the field between its plates is $E$. Which statements about the force between the plates are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Each plate feels only the field of the other plate
questions.explanation: A plate doesn't push on itself, so it feels only the other plate's field, $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0) = E/2$. The force is $Q\cdot E/2 = Q^2/(2\varepsilon_0A)$, an attraction between opposite charges. $QE$ is double the right value.

questions.stem: Match each expression to what it gives.
choices: Self-energy of a thin charged shell
Self-energy of a uniformly charged ball
Outward pressure on a charged conductor
Field just outside a charged conductor
questions.explanation: The shell has field only outside; the ball has field inside too, so $\tfrac35 > \tfrac12$. The surface pressure is $\sigma^2/(2\varepsilon_0)$ (force per area), and multiplying it by the plate area gives $Q^2/(2\varepsilon_0A)$. The field just outside a conductor is $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, without the square and the $\tfrac12$.

questions.stem: All four objects carry the same charge $Q$. Rank their self-energies from smallest to largest.
choices: A thin shell of radius R
A uniform ball of radius R
questions.explanation: In units of $kQ^2/R$: shell $2R$, $1/4 = 0.25$; ball $2R$, $3/10 = 0.30$; shell $R$, $0.50$; ball $R$, $0.60$. Squeezing the same charge into a smaller space costs more energy, and a ball costs 1.2 times a shell of the same size.

questions.stem: A capacitor stays connected to a battery while its plates are pulled apart. A student uses $F = -dU/dx$ with $U = \varepsilon_0AV^2/(2x)$. What does the student wrongly conclude?
choices: That the force is twice too large but attractive
That the force grows with the gap
questions.explanation: $-dU/dx = +\varepsilon_0AV^2/(2x^2)$, positive: a push toward larger $x$, a repulsion. At fixed $V$ the battery also does work ($2\,dU$), and the correct rule is $F = +dU/dx = -\varepsilon_0AV^2/(2x^2)$, an attraction of the right size.

questions.stem: Plates of area 0.010 m² are 2.0 mm apart and held at 400 V. The force between them is ___ mN (2 significant figures). Give only the number.
Just outside a charged conductor the field is $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$. Why is the force per area on the surface charge only $\sigma^2/(2\varepsilon_0)$?
choices: Half the charge is inside the conductor, where the field is zero
The surface charge feels the average of the field inside (zero) and just outside
The field is $\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ everywhere outside a conductor
The conductor's atoms hold back half of the force
questions.explanation: Across the thin layer of charge the field climbs from 0 to $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$, and integrating $\rho E$ through the layer gives $\sigma\cdot\sigma/(2\varepsilon_0)$ whatever the layer's profile. All the excess charge is on the surface, and the outside field is the full $\sigma/\varepsilon_0$.

questions.stem: A uniform wire runs from a higher-potential end (+) to a lower-potential end (−). Name the numbered features.

image.alt: A cylindrical wire between a + end on the left and a − end on the right, with electrons drawn inside. Marker 1 is at the circular end face, marker 2 on a bracket under the whole wire, marker 3 on an arrow above the wire pointing from + to −, and marker 4 on an arrow below the wire pointing from − to +.

questions.explanation: Conventional current points the way positive charge would move, from the + (high-potential) end to the − end. The electrons that really carry current in a metal are negative, so they drift the opposite way. The end face is the area $A$ and the bracket the length $L$ in $R = \rho L/A$. Resistivity is a property of the material, not a feature you can point to.

questions.stem: The current in a wire is $I(t) = 6.0e^{-t/3}$ A for $t \ge 0$ (t in seconds). The total charge that ever passes through it is ___ C. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: $Q = \int_0^\infty 6.0e^{-t/3}\,dt = 6.0 \times 3 = 18$ C: the area under the $I$–$t$ graph. Multiplying the starting current by 1 s instead of integrating gives 6.0, which is not the charge.

questions.stem: Match each expression to the quantity it gives.
choices: Power turned to heat in a resistor
questions.explanation: $I = nqv_dA$ counts the charge crossing a section per second; $R = \rho L/A$ is the resistance of a wire; $\vec J = \vec E/\rho$ is Ohm's law in local form; $P = I^2R$ is Joule heating. None of them is a capacitor's charge ($Q = CV$).

questions.stem: A heating element made of a single wire runs on a fixed 120 V outlet. Ignoring changes in temperature, which changes would increase the power it produces? Select all that apply.
choices: Using a shorter piece of the same wire
Using a thicker wire of the same material and length
Using a material with a higher resistivity, same size
Using a wire twice as long
questions.explanation: At fixed voltage $P = V^2/R$, so anything that lowers $R = \rho L/A$ raises the power. A shorter wire (smaller $L$) and a thicker one (larger $A$) both lower $R$. Higher resistivity or more length raise $R$ and lower the power. (The rule "more resistance, more heat" holds only at fixed current, $P = I^2R$.)

questions.stem: A copper resistor ($\rho = 1.7\times10^{-8}$ Ω·m) is a cone 0.10 m long whose radius tapers from 1.0 mm to 2.0 mm. Using $R = \rho L/(\pi ab)$, what is its resistance?
questions.explanation: $R = \dfrac{(1.7\times10^{-8})(0.10)}{\pi(1.0\times10^{-3})(2.0\times10^{-3})} = 2.7\times10^{-4}$ Ω. Using the average radius 1.5 mm gives $2.4\times10^{-4}$ Ω (close, but not the exact integral); using only the small radius gives $5.4\times10^{-4}$ Ω and only the large radius $1.4\times10^{-4}$ Ω.

questions.stem: A circuit is set up to measure the current through a resistor and the voltage across it. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A circuit loop. Marker 1 is beside a symbol with a long and a short plate on the left side. Marker 2 is at a lever between two contacts on the top wire. Marker 3 is at a blank meter circle on the top wire, in line with everything else. Marker 4 is beside a zigzag between the top and bottom wires. Marker 5 is beside a second blank meter circle connected across the two ends of the zigzag.

questions.explanation: The long-and-short plate symbol is a battery and the lever is a switch. The meter in line with the loop (in series) carries the same current as the resistor, so it is the ammeter. The meter connected across the resistor's two ends (in parallel) has the same voltage as the resistor, so it is the voltmeter.

questions.stem: A 4.0 Ω resistor is in series with a parallel pair of 3.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω, connected to an ideal 12 V battery. The equivalent resistance is ___ Ω and the battery current is ___ A. (Give only the numbers.)
questions.explanation: Parallel pair: $\dfrac{3.0(6.0)}{3.0 + 6.0} = 2.0$ Ω. In series with 4.0 Ω: $R_{\text{eq}} = 6.0$ Ω. Battery current $I = 12/6.0 = 2.0$ A.

questions.stem: Three identical 6.0 Ω resistors can be connected in four ways. Put the combinations in order of equivalent resistance, smallest first.
choices: Two in series, that pair in parallel with the third
Two in parallel, that pair in series with the third
questions.explanation: All parallel: $6/3 = 2$ Ω. A series pair (12 Ω) in parallel with 6 Ω: $\dfrac{12(6)}{18} = 4$ Ω. A parallel pair (3 Ω) in series with 6 Ω: 9 Ω. All series: 18 Ω.

questions.stem: A battery with emf $\mathcal{E}$ and internal resistance $r$ is connected to a variable load resistor $R$. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.
choices: The terminal voltage is less than $\mathcal{E}$ whenever current flows
With no load connected, the terminal voltage equals $\mathcal{E}$
Making $R$ smaller always increases the power delivered to the load
When $R = r$, half of the emf appears across the load
questions.explanation: $V = \mathcal{E} - Ir$, so the terminal voltage drops below $\mathcal{E}$ whenever $I \ne 0$ and equals it when $I = 0$. At $R = r$, $I = \mathcal{E}/(2r)$ and the load voltage is $IR = \mathcal{E}/2$. Load power $\mathcal{E}^2R/(R + r)^2$ peaks at $R = r$; making $R$ smaller than $r$ lowers it again (it is zero for a short circuit).

questions.stem: Match each arrangement to the property that defines it.
choices: In series and very low resistance
In parallel and very high resistance
questions.explanation: Series parts share one path, so one current; parallel parts connect across the same two points, so one voltage. An ammeter goes in series and must barely change the current (low resistance); a voltmeter goes in parallel and must draw almost no current (high resistance). Equal power is not a general property of either arrangement.

questions.stem: In the circuit of Example 3 (shown), the 6.0 Ω branch is cut, leaving the two battery branches in one loop. What current flows around the loop?

image.alt: Three vertical branches between junctions A (top) and B (bottom): a 12 V battery and 2.0 Ω resistor, a 6.0 V battery and 3.0 Ω resistor, both with the + plate toward A, and a 6.0 Ω resistor alone.

questions.explanation: The batteries oppose each other around the loop (both $+$ terminals face A), so the net emf is $12 - 6.0 = 6.0$ V across $2.0 + 3.0 = 5.0$ Ω: $I = 1.2$ A, up through the 12 V branch and down through the 6.0 V one. Adding the emfs gives 3.6 A; 2.0 A is the old $I_1$; 6.0 A is 12 V over 2.0 Ω alone.

questions.stem: This circuit can both charge and discharge a capacitor. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: A circuit loop. Marker 1 is beside a symbol with one long and one short plate on the left side. Marker 2 is above a two-way lever on the top wire, whose second contact leads straight down to the bottom wire. Marker 3 is above a zigzag on the top wire. Marker 4 is beside a symbol with two equal parallel plates on the right side.

questions.explanation: Unequal plates are a battery (long plate +); equal plates are a capacitor; the zigzag is the resistor. The two-way switch connects the RC pair either to the battery (charging) or straight across itself (discharging through the same resistor).

questions.stem: A capacitor discharging through a resistor has a half-life of 0.35 s. Its voltage falls from 16 V to 2.0 V in ___ s. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 V is three halvings, so $t = 3(0.35) = 1.05$ s. (Check: $t = \tau\ln 8$ with $\tau = 0.35/\ln 2 = 0.505$ s gives 1.05 s.)

questions.stem: A capacitor charges from zero through a resistor. Put these moments in time order, earliest first.
choices: It has half its final charge
It has 63% of its final charge
It has 86% of its final charge
It has 99% of its final charge
questions.explanation: From $q/Q = 1 - e^{-t/RC}$, $t = -RC\ln(1 - q/Q)$: half at $0.69RC$, 63% at $RC$, 86% at $2RC$, 99% at about $4.6RC$.

questions.stem: A battery, a resistor $R$ and an uncharged capacitor $C$ are in series. Which statements describe the instant just after the switch closes? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: An uncharged capacitor has no voltage, and its voltage cannot jump, so at first it acts like a wire: the whole emf is across $R$ and $I = \mathcal{E}/R$. Zero current and charge $C\mathcal{E}$ describe the end of charging, long after the switch closes.

questions.stem: Match each expression to what it gives for an RC circuit with battery emf $\mathcal{E}$.
choices: Time for a discharge to halve the charge
Energy the battery supplies during a full charge
Crossover frequency of an RC filter
questions.explanation: $\tau = RC$; the half-life is $RC\ln 2$; the current starts at $\mathcal{E}/R$; the battery moves $Q = C\mathcal{E}$ through $\mathcal{E}$, supplying $C\mathcal{E}^2$ (half is stored, half heats $R$); RC filters cross over near $1/(2\pi RC)$. The final charging current is zero, which none of these expressions gives.

questions.stem: In Example 1 of the RC lesson (4.0 μF, 50 kΩ, 12 V, so $\tau = 0.20$ s and $I_0 = 0.24$ mA), what is the current at $t = 0.30$ s?
questions.explanation: $I = I_0e^{-t/\tau} = 0.24e^{-1.5} = 0.054$ mA. Using the charge's shape $1 - e^{-t/\tau}$ gives 0.19 mA; 0.24 mA is the starting current; 0.11 mA comes from doubling the time constant to 0.40 s.

questions.stem: A linear network and its two equivalents. Name the numbered parts.

image.alt: Three circuits joined by equals signs: a box labeled batteries and resistors with terminals a and b; a Thévenin equivalent with a battery (marker 1) and a resistor on the top wire (marker 2); and a Norton equivalent with a circle containing an upward arrow (marker 3) and a resistor connected across it between the top and bottom wires (marker 4).

choices: Battery equal to the open-circuit voltage
Resistor in series with the source
Resistor in parallel with the source
questions.explanation: Thévenin: a battery $V_{\text{th}}$ (the open-circuit voltage) in series with $R_{\text{th}}$. Norton: a current source $I_N$ (the short-circuit current) in parallel with the same $R_{\text{th}}$. No load is attached in the picture; the terminals a and b are where one would go.

questions.stem: A network has 5 nodes (junctions) and 8 branches. How many unknown potentials does the node-voltage method need?
questions.explanation: One node is the reference at zero potential, leaving $5 - 1 = 4$ unknowns. The branch-current method would need 8 unknowns, one per branch; 5 forgets the reference node.

questions.stem: Three branches join node A to the reference node B: a 10 V battery ($+$ toward A) in series with 2.0 Ω, a 4.0 Ω resistor, and another 4.0 Ω resistor. The potential of A is ___ V. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: Junction rule at A: $\dfrac{10 - V}{2.0} = \dfrac{V}{4.0} + \dfrac{V}{4.0}$, so $10 - V = V$ and $V = 5.0$ V. (Check: the two 4.0 Ω resistors make 2.0 Ω, an equal divider of 10 V.)

questions.stem: An ideal 12 V battery drives $R_1 = 4.0$ kΩ and $R_2 = 12$ kΩ in series. Terminals a and b are across $R_2$. What are the Thévenin voltage and resistance seen from a and b?
questions.explanation: Open circuit: $V_{\text{th}} = 12\cdot\dfrac{12}{16} = 9.0$ V. Battery replaced by a wire: $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in parallel between a and b, $R_{\text{th}} = \dfrac{4(12)}{16} = 3.0$ kΩ. 16 kΩ adds them in series; 3.0 V is the voltage across $R_1$; 12 V ignores the divider.

questions.stem: A 6.0 kΩ load is connected to the terminals of the previous divider ($V_{\text{th}} = 9.0$ V, $R_{\text{th}} = 3.0$ kΩ). What current flows through the load?
questions.explanation: $I = \dfrac{9.0}{3.0 + 6.0} = 1.0$ mA (so the load has 6.0 V across it, not 9.0 V). Ignoring $R_{\text{th}}$ gives 1.5 mA; 0.75 mA is the divider current with no load; 3.0 mA is the Norton (short-circuit) current.

questions.stem: What is the Norton current of the same divider (12 V, 4.0 kΩ, 12 kΩ, terminals across the 12 kΩ)?
questions.explanation: A wire across a and b shorts out $R_2$, so $I_N = 12/4.0 = 3.0$ mA, which equals $V_{\text{th}}/R_{\text{th}} = 9.0/3.0$. 0.75 mA is the divider current with nothing connected; 0.56 mA divides $V_{\text{th}}$ by $R_1 + R_2$ instead of by $R_{\text{th}}$.

questions.stem: Which statements about the Thévenin resistance $R_{\text{th}}$ of a linear network are true? Select all that apply.
choices: It equals the open-circuit voltage divided by the short-circuit current
It is found with every ideal battery replaced by a wire
It is found with every ideal battery removed, leaving a gap
It changes with the load resistance connected to the terminals
questions.explanation: $R_{\text{th}} = V_{\text{oc}}/I_{\text{sc}}$, and it is the resistance between the terminals with each ideal emf set to zero, which means a wire (an ideal battery has no internal resistance). Leaving a gap would cut whole branches out. $R_{\text{th}}$ is a property of the network alone, not of the load.

questions.stem: In a two-battery circuit, each battery acting alone would drive 2.0 A through a 5.0 Ω resistor, in the same direction. What power does the resistor dissipate with both batteries in place?
questions.explanation: Superposition adds currents: $I = 2.0 + 2.0 = 4.0$ A, so $P = I^2R = 16(5.0) = 80$ W. Adding the separate powers ($20 + 20$) gives 40 W, the classic mistake: power is quadratic in current.

questions.stem: Ladders of equal resistors $R$ (series $R$, then shunt $R$, repeated) are measured from their input terminals. Put them in order of resistance, smallest first.
questions.explanation: One section: $2R$. Two: $R + (R\parallel2R) = 1.667R$. Three: $1.625R$. Infinite: $\tfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2}R = 1.618R$. Each added section puts another resistor in parallel with the end, lowering the total toward the golden-ratio limit.

questions.stem: A Wheatstone bridge balances (zero galvanometer current) with $R_1 = 200$ Ω, $R_2 = 300$ Ω and $R_3 = 400$ Ω. Using $R_1/R_2 = R_3/R_x$, what is $R_x$?
questions.explanation: $R_x = \dfrac{R_2R_3}{R_1} = \dfrac{300(400)}{200} = 600$ Ω. Inverting the ratio gives $R_1R_3/R_2 = 267$ Ω; $R_1R_2/R_3 = 150$ Ω; 900 Ω just adds the three.

questions.stem: Why can a Wheatstone bridge measure resistance more precisely than reading a voltmeter and an ammeter?
choices: At balance the result depends only on the other resistors, not on the emf or a meter's calibration
Its battery has no internal resistance
It uses alternating current, which avoids heating
questions.explanation: At balance $R_x = R_2R_3/R_1$: the emf cancels out and the galvanometer only has to detect zero current (a null measurement), so its calibration does not matter. The galvanometer has some resistance, the battery's internal resistance doesn't affect balance, and a basic bridge runs on DC.

questions.stem: An infinite ladder is built from 2.0 Ω resistors. Its input resistance is ___ Ω. (Give 3 significant figures.)
questions.explanation: $R_\infty = \dfrac{1 + \sqrt5}{2}R = 1.618(2.0) = 3.24$ Ω, from $R_\infty = R + \dfrac{RR_\infty}{R + R_\infty}$.

questions.stem: Match each method to its key idea.
choices: Unknowns are the potentials at the junctions
A battery in series with one resistor
A current source in parallel with one resistor
Adds the effects of each source acting alone
Adds the powers from each source
questions.explanation: Node voltages use junction potentials (the loop rule is automatic); Kirchhoff's branch method uses branch currents; Thévenin and Norton replace a network by a series battery-resistor or a parallel source-resistor; superposition adds currents and voltages, never powers.

questions.stem: Repeat Example 3 of the network lesson with $R_x = 90$ Ω instead of 110 Ω ($\mathcal{E} = 10$ V, $R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = 100$ Ω, $R_g = 50$ Ω). What is the galvanometer current?
questions.explanation: $V_d = 10(90/190) = 4.737$ V, so $|V_{\text{th}}| = 5.000 - 4.737 = 0.263$ V (now c is higher). $R_{\text{th}} = 50 + \dfrac{100(90)}{190} = 97.4$ Ω. $I_g = \dfrac{0.263}{97.4 + 50} = 1.79$ mA. Leaving out $R_g$ gives 2.70 mA; dividing by $R_g$ alone gives 5.26 mA; 1.56 mA is the 110 Ω answer.

questions.stem: Name the numbered parts of this RC low-pass filter.

image.alt: A two-port circuit. Marker 1 is between a pair of open terminals on the left, marker 2 is above a zigzag on the top wire, marker 3 is beside a pair of equal parallel plates connected from the top wire to the bottom wire, and marker 4 is between a pair of open terminals on the right.

questions.explanation: The signal enters on the left, passes through the resistor, and the output is taken across the capacitor. Fast changes cannot charge the capacitor in time, so they barely reach the output: a low-pass filter.

questions.stem: An ideal 12 V battery, a switch and $R_1 = 4.0$ kΩ are in series with a parallel pair: $R_2 = 12$ kΩ and a 5.0 μF capacitor. What is the time constant after the switch closes?
questions.explanation: From the capacitor's terminals, with the battery replaced by a wire, $R_1$ and $R_2$ are in parallel: $R_{\text{th}} = 3.0$ kΩ, so $\tau = (3.0\text{ k}\Omega)(5.0\ \mu\text{F}) = 15$ ms. 80 ms uses $R_1 + R_2$; 20 ms uses $R_1$ alone; 60 ms uses $R_2$ alone.

questions.stem: In the same circuit (12 V, $R_1 = 4.0$ kΩ in series, $R_2 = 12$ kΩ in parallel with the capacitor), the capacitor's voltage long after the switch closes is ___ V. (Give only the number.)
questions.explanation: In steady state the capacitor carries no current, so $R_1$ and $R_2$ form a divider: $V_C = 12\cdot\dfrac{12}{16} = 9.0$ V. It does not reach the full 12 V because $R_2$ keeps drawing current through $R_1$.

questions.stem: In the same circuit, what is the battery current just after the switch closes?
questions.explanation: The uncharged capacitor's voltage cannot jump, so at $0^+$ it acts as a wire and shorts $R_2$: $I = 12/4.0 = 3.0$ mA. The current then decays toward the steady value $12/16 = 0.75$ mA.

questions.stem: A switch is thrown in a circuit of resistors, batteries and one capacitor. Which quantities can change suddenly (jump) at that instant? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A jump in the capacitor's voltage (or charge, $q = CV_C$) would need $I = C\,dV_C/dt$ to be infinite, so these are continuous. Resistor currents and voltages have no such limit and can jump, as the battery current does at $t = 0$.

questions.stem: A relaxation oscillator has $\mathcal{E} = 10$ V, $V_{\text{on}} = 7.0$ V, $V_{\text{off}} = 2.0$ V and $RC = 10$ ms, with an instant discharge. What is its period?
questions.explanation: $T = RC\ln\dfrac{\mathcal{E} - V_{\text{off}}}{\mathcal{E} - V_{\text{on}}} = 10\ln\dfrac{8.0}{3.0} = 9.81$ ms. Using $\ln(V_{\text{on}}/V_{\text{off}})$ gives 12.5 ms; 12.0 ms is the first cycle starting from 0 V, $10\ln(10/3)$; 10.0 ms is just $RC$.

questions.stem: Put one cycle of a relaxation oscillator in order, starting just as the threshold switch opens.
choices: The switch opens with the capacitor at the lower threshold
The capacitor charges through the resistor toward the emf
The capacitor voltage reaches the upper threshold
The switch closes and the capacitor discharges quickly
questions.explanation: The switch opens at $V_{\text{off}}$; the capacitor charges toward $\mathcal{E}$ along an exponential; at $V_{\text{on}}$ the switch closes and dumps the charge back down to $V_{\text{off}}$, where the next cycle starts.

questions.stem: What is the cutoff frequency of an RC filter with $R = 4.7$ kΩ and $C = 10$ nF?
questions.explanation: $f_c = \dfrac{1}{2\pi RC} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi(4.7\times10^3)(10\times10^{-9})} = 3.39$ kHz. Forgetting the $2\pi$ gives $1/RC = 21.3$ kHz (an angular frequency in s⁻¹, not a frequency in Hz); $1/(\pi RC) = 6.77$ kHz uses $\pi$ instead of $2\pi$; 0.339 kHz slips a power of ten in the nanofarads.

questions.stem: At its cutoff frequency, an RC low-pass filter's gain $V_{\text{out}}/V_{\text{in}}$ is ___ . (Give 3 decimal places.)
questions.explanation: At $f = f_c$, $\omega RC = 1$, so the gain is $1/\sqrt{1 + 1} = 1/\sqrt2 = 0.707$ and the output power is half the low-frequency value.

questions.stem: An RC high-pass filter (output across the resistor) is driven at twice its cutoff frequency. What is its gain?
questions.explanation: High-pass gain $= \dfrac{\omega RC}{\sqrt{1 + (\omega RC)^2}}$ with $\omega RC = 2$: $2/\sqrt5 = 0.894$. 0.447 is the low-pass gain at the same frequency; 0.707 is the gain at the cutoff; 0.500 is $1/(\omega RC)$, the high-frequency approximation of the low-pass gain.

questions.stem: Match each situation to what the capacitor acts like.
left: Uncharged capacitor just after a switch closes
Capacitor in a DC circuit long after switching
Charged capacitor just after its battery is removed
Capacitor in a low-pass filter at very high frequency
choices: A battery at its present voltage
questions.explanation: A capacitor's voltage can't jump, so at the instant of switching it holds whatever voltage it had: zero (a wire) or its present voltage (a battery). In steady DC it carries no current (a break). At very high frequency it barely changes voltage over a cycle, so it acts nearly as a wire and shorts the output.

questions.stem: A 6.0 μF capacitor charged to 50 V is connected through a resistor to an uncharged 3.0 μF capacitor. What are the final voltage and the energy turned into heat?
questions.explanation: Charge is conserved: $V_f = \dfrac{6.0(50)}{9.0} = 33$ V. Heat $= \tfrac12\dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1 + C_2}V_0^2 = \tfrac12(2.0\ \mu\text{F})(50)^2 = 2.5$ mJ (7.5 mJ before, 5.0 mJ after). Averaging the voltages gives 25 V; "zero" assumes energy is conserved, which it is not; 50 V assumes the first capacitor keeps its voltage, which would need charge to appear from nowhere.

questions.stem: When two capacitors share charge through a resistor, why is the heat produced the same whatever the resistance?
choices: The resistor heats only at the instant of connection
A smaller resistance gives a larger current for a shorter time, and the integral of $I^2R$ comes out the same
Resistance has no effect on current in a capacitor circuit
The capacitors absorb the extra energy as charge
questions.explanation: $I = (V_0/R)e^{-t/RC_s}$, so $\int_0^\infty I^2R\,dt = \dfrac{V_0^2}{R}\cdot\dfrac{RC_s}{2} = \tfrac12C_sV_0^2$: $R$ cancels. $R$ sets how fast the energy goes, not how much.

questions.stem: An RC low-pass filter is driven at ten times its cutoff frequency. What is its gain, to 3 significant figures?
questions.explanation: $\omega RC = 10$, so the gain is $1/\sqrt{101} = 0.0995$, very close to $f_c/f = 0.1$. 0.0100 squares the ratio (that's roughly the power ratio); 0.995 is the high-pass gain $10/\sqrt{101}$; 0.707 is the gain at the cutoff.

glossary.definition: Of a vector field: the outward flux per unit volume around a point, $\nabla\cdot\vec E = \partial E_x/\partial x + \partial E_y/\partial y + \partial E_z/\partial z$. Positive at a source, negative at a sink.
For any closed surface, the outward flux of a field equals the integral of its divergence over the enclosed volume: $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec A = \int(\nabla\cdot\vec E)\,dV$.
Of a vector field: a vector whose components give the circulation per unit area around small loops perpendicular to each axis; it measures how much the field swirls around a point.
The circulation of a field around a closed loop equals the flux of its curl through any surface bounded by the loop: $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = \int(\nabla\times\vec E)\cdot d\vec A$.
Local charge conservation: $\nabla\cdot\vec J + \partial\rho/\partial t = 0$. Charge in a small volume decreases only by flowing out through its surface.

The equation $\nabla^2f = \dfrac{1}{v^2}\dfrac{\partial^2f}{\partial t^2}$, whose solutions are waves traveling at speed $v$. Maxwell's equations in vacuum give it for $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ with $v = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0} = c$.
A wave whose fields depend only on time and on distance along one direction, so the wavefronts are flat planes. An electromagnetic plane wave in vacuum is transverse, with $E = cB$.
The fact that every inertial observer measures the same electric charge on a particle or object, whatever its speed.

The rules for how $\vec E$ and $\vec B$ change between frames moving at relative velocity $\vec v$: components along $\vec v$ are unchanged; $\vec E'_\perp = \gamma(\vec E + \vec v\times\vec B)_\perp$ and $\vec B'_\perp = \gamma(\vec B - \vec v\times\vec E/c^2)_\perp$.
The combinations $\vec E\cdot\vec B$ and $E^2 - c^2B^2$, which have the same value in every inertial frame.
The part of an accelerated charge's field that breaks free and travels outward at $c$: transverse, of size $qa\sin\theta/(4\pi\varepsilon_0c^2r)$, falling off as $1/r$.
The total power radiated by a charge $q$ with acceleration $a$, moving slowly compared with $c$: $P = q^2a^2/(6\pi\varepsilon_0c^3)$.
Radiation from charges moving in curved paths in magnetic fields, especially fast electrons in storage rings; used as an intense X-ray source.
German for "braking radiation": radiation, usually X-rays with a continuous spread of energies, from charges decelerated as they pass atoms, as in an X-ray tube.
Scattering of light by particles much smaller than the wavelength, such as air molecules; in the simple model its strength goes as $1/\lambda^4$, which is why the sky is blue.
In Bohr's model, the allowed orbits in which an electron does not radiate, contrary to classical electromagnetism; light is emitted only in jumps between them.

Bohr's requirement that quantum predictions agree with classical physics in the limit of large quantum numbers; for hydrogen, the $n \to n - 1$ photon frequency approaches the classical orbital frequency.
The four numbers $P = (E/c, p_x, p_y, p_z)$, which transform between frames like $(ct, x, y, z)$. Its square $P\cdot P = E^2/c^2 - p^2 = m^2c^2$ is the same in every frame.

Of a system of particles: $M$ with $M^2c^4 = (\sum E)^2 - |\sum\vec pc|^2$, the same in every frame. $Mc^2$ is the total energy in the center-of-momentum frame; it is generally not the sum of the particles' masses.
The frame in which the total momentum of a system is zero; there its total energy equals $Mc^2$, the energy available to make new particles.
The antiparticle of the electron: the same mass, charge $+e$.
The creation of a particle and its antiparticle, such as an electron and a positron from a gamma ray near a nucleus (threshold about 1.022 MeV).
The minimum beam energy that can produce a given reaction; for a beam of mass $m_b$ on a target $m_t$ at rest making products of total mass $M$, $K_{\text{th}} = [M^2 - (m_b + m_t)^2]c^2/(2m_t)$.
Two identical coaxial coils of radius $R$, carrying the same current in the same direction and separated by $R$; near the midpoint the field is very uniform, $B = (4/5)^{3/2}\mu_0NI/R$.
A coil wound on a ring-shaped (doughnut) core. Inside the windings $B = \mu_0NI/(2\pi r)$; outside, the field is zero.

Describes a field whose work on a charge around any closed path is zero ($\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = 0$), so that a potential can be defined. Fields made by static charges are conservative; induced electric fields are not.
An electric field produced by a changing magnetic flux, with closed field lines and $\oint\vec E\cdot d\vec\ell = -d\Phi_B/dt$. It is not conservative, so it has no potential.
A circular accelerator in which an increasing magnetic field's induced electric field speeds electrons up while the field at the orbit steers them; it requires $B_{\text{orbit}} = \tfrac12\bar B$.
The emf induced in a motor's spinning coil, which opposes the supply voltage and grows with speed: $I = (V - \mathcal{E}_b)/R$.
A rotating arrow representing a sinusoidal quantity: its length is the amplitude, its angle the phase. Sinusoids of the same frequency add as their phasors add, like vectors.
For a series RLC circuit, $Q = \omega_0L/R = \dfrac1R\sqrt{L/C}$; in general $2\pi$ times the energy stored divided by the energy lost per cycle. A high $Q$ means a sharp resonance.
The two frequencies at which a driven resonant circuit absorbs half its maximum average power; for a series RLC circuit, where $|X_L - X_C| = R$.
The width of a resonance between its half-power points: $\Delta\omega = R/L = \omega_0/Q$ for a series RLC circuit (and $\Delta f = f_0/Q$).

The center of the sphere of which a curved mirror or lens surface is part, a distance $R$ (the radius of curvature) from the surface; for a spherical mirror the focal point lies halfway to it, $f = R/2$.
An instrument that splits light into two beams, sends them along different paths and recombines them, reading tiny path differences (fractions of a wavelength) from the interference fringes.
A partly reflecting plate that reflects about half of a light beam and transmits the rest, dividing it into two beams (and later recombining them in an interferometer).
One bright or dark band of an interference pattern. In a Michelson interferometer one fringe passes for each wavelength of change in the path difference.
The geometric length a ray travels times the index of refraction, $nL$; it counts how many wavelengths fit along the path and is what decides interference.
The largest path difference over which light from a source still forms visible fringes, roughly $\lambda^2/\Delta\lambda$: about 1 μm for white light, meters for a good laser.
How fast the angle of a grating maximum changes with wavelength, $d\theta/d\lambda = m/(d\cos\theta)$; it says how far apart two colors land.
For a grating, $R = \lambda/\Delta\lambda = Nm$: the ratio of a wavelength to the smallest wavelength difference that can be separated, set by the number of lines illuminated times the order.
In X-ray diffraction, the angle $\theta$ between the incoming beam and the crystal planes (not the normal); the beam is deflected by $2\theta$.
The condition $2d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for strong X-ray reflection from crystal planes a distance $d$ apart, with $\theta$ the glancing angle.
Finding how the atoms in a crystal are arranged from the angles and strengths of its X-ray diffraction peaks, using Bragg's law.

Any way a real lens or mirror fails to bring all rays from one object point to a single image point, mainly because the small-angle approximation breaks down (spherical aberration) or the index depends on wavelength (chromatic aberration).

The 2 × 2 matrix $\begin{pmatrix} A & B \\ C & D \end{pmatrix}$ that takes a paraxial ray's height and angle at the input of an optical system to their values at the output; it is the product of the matrices of the elements, the first one on the right.
The distance from the last surface of an optical system to the point where incoming parallel rays focus, $-A/C$ from the system matrix.
The focal length of the single thin lens that would make images of distant objects the same size as an optical system does; $f = -1/C$ for a system in air.
A lens system, typically a converging group followed by a diverging one, whose effective focal length is longer than the distance from its front to its focus: a long focal length in a short barrel.
The blur caused by spherical surfaces focusing rays far from the axis closer than rays near it; reduced by smaller apertures, aspheric surfaces or, for mirrors, a paraboloidal shape.
The color blur caused by dispersion: a lens has a shorter focal length for violet light than for red. Mirrors don't have it.
A glass's measure of dispersion, $V = (n_d - 1)/(n_F - n_C)$ using indices at 587.6 nm, 486.1 nm and 656.3 nm; a large $V$ means low dispersion.
A converging crown-glass lens cemented to a weaker diverging flint-glass lens so that their color errors cancel, $P_1/V_1 + P_2/V_2 = 0$, while their powers add.
Space and time together, treated as one four-dimensional geometry in which different observers slice time and space differently but agree on the spacetime interval.
A graph with position $x$ across and $ct$ up. Light travels at $45^\circ$; an object at rest is a vertical line.
Something that happens at one place at one instant: a single point in spacetime, given by $(x, t)$ in a chosen frame.
The line on a spacetime diagram traced by an object through all the events of its history.
The $45^\circ$ lines (a cone in more dimensions) through an event, traced by light. Only events inside or on its future half can be affected by the event.
The quantity $(\Delta s)^2 = (c\Delta t)^2 - (\Delta x)^2$ between two events, the same in every inertial frame. For timelike separations, $\Delta s/c$ is the proper time.
Describes two events with $(\Delta s)^2 > 0$: a clock moving slower than light can be present at both, and all observers agree on their order.
Describes two events with $(\Delta s)^2 < 0$: no signal can connect them, some frame sees them as simultaneous, and observers can disagree about their order.
Describes two events with $(\Delta s)^2 = 0$: only a light signal can connect them.
A shift of light to longer wavelengths, as from a receding source; measured by $z = \lambda_{\text{obs}}/\lambda_{\text{src}} - 1$. A shift to shorter wavelengths is a blueshift.
The change in observed frequency of light from a moving source: $\lambda_{\text{obs}} = \lambda_{\text{src}}\sqrt{(1 + \beta)/(1 - \beta)}$ for a receding source, with $\beta$ reversed for approach.
The redshift, by the factor $\gamma$, of light from a source moving at right angles to the line of sight; it comes purely from time dilation and has no counterpart for sound.
The passage of a particle through a region where its energy is less than the potential energy, which is impossible classically but has a nonzero probability in quantum mechanics.
The place where a particle's potential energy equals its total energy, so a classical particle stops and reverses there.
A region where $U > E$, so the kinetic energy would be negative; classical particles never enter it, but the quantum wave function decays into it.
The distance $1/\kappa$ over which a wave function decaying as $e^{-\kappa x}$ inside a barrier falls by a factor of $e$; $\kappa = \sqrt{2m(U - E)}/\hbar$.
The probability $T$ that a particle gets through a barrier; for a thick barrier $T \approx 16\frac{E}{U}(1 - \frac{E}{U})e^{-2\kappa L}$.
A microscope that images a conducting surface atom by atom by holding a sharp tip a fraction of a nanometer away and measuring the tunneling current, which changes about tenfold per 0.1 nm of gap.
The current of electrons tunneling across a thin gap or insulating layer; it is roughly proportional to $e^{-2\kappa d}$ for a gap $d$.

The empirical rule (1911) that alpha emitters with higher alpha energies have much shorter half-lives; in modern form, log(half-life) falls roughly linearly with $1/\sqrt{E_\alpha}$. Tunneling theory explains it.
The energy released in a nuclear reaction or decay: $Q = (\sum m_{\text{initial}} - \sum m_{\text{final}})c^2$. Positive Q releases energy.
Describes a reaction with $Q > 0$, which releases energy as kinetic energy of the products.
Describes a reaction with $Q < 0$, which can occur only if the colliding particles supply kinetic energy (somewhat more than $|Q|$).
A formula for nuclear binding energy based on treating the nucleus as a charged liquid drop: $E_B = a_VA - a_SA^{2/3} - a_CZ(Z - 1)/A^{1/3} - a_A(A - 2Z)^2/A \pm \delta$, with fitted coefficients.
The term $a_VA$ in the semi-empirical mass formula: binding proportional to the number of nucleons, because each is bound to its nearest neighbors.
The term $-a_SA^{2/3}$ in the semi-empirical mass formula: nucleons at the surface have fewer neighbors, which lowers the binding, most of all for light nuclei.
The term $-a_CZ(Z - 1)/A^{1/3}$ in the semi-empirical mass formula: the electric repulsion between every pair of protons, which lowers the binding most for heavy nuclei.
The term $-a_A(A - 2Z)^2/A$ in the semi-empirical mass formula: by the exclusion principle, an excess of neutrons or protons must occupy higher energy levels.
The term $\pm\delta$ in the semi-empirical mass formula: extra binding for even $Z$ and even $N$, less for odd $Z$ and odd $N$, zero for odd $A$.
$\nabla^2V = -\rho/\varepsilon_0$: Gauss's law written for the potential, linking how $V$ curves to the charge density.
$\nabla^2V = 0$, Poisson's equation in a region with no charge. Its solutions have no local maximum or minimum.
No charged particle can be held in stable equilibrium by electrostatic forces from fixed charges alone, because the potential has no local minimum or maximum in empty space.
With the charge in a region and the potential on all its boundaries given, Laplace's or Poisson's equation has exactly one solution, so any solution that fits is the solution.
A fictitious charge placed outside the region of interest so that, together with the real charges, it gives a conductor's surface the right potential.
